# The AI-Assisted Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** George E. P. Box used this aphorism about statistical
models. Every model simplifies, and the working question is whether the
simplification still serves the decision at hand. A
task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite always leaves
something out. Each can still be useful when its scope and failure modes are
clear and when the decision does not reach beyond the evidence it provides.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
AI can generate more candidates and invoke more tools than an architect can
inspect by hand. How should that work be organized so that promising outputs
become defensible design decisions rather than a larger pile of plausible
results?
:::

Architecture work combines explicit artifacts with what Michael Polanyi called
tacit knowledge [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension]. Requirements, traces, models,
register-transfer-level (RTL) descriptions, floorplans, and review notes record
part of the work. Experienced architects supply the rest from memory. They know
which workload phases count, which model is stale, which constraint is
provisional, which tool warning is harmless, and which favorable result
contradicts physical experience.

AI assistance changes the volume and pace of this work without removing those
judgments. A system can propose hundreds of candidates, write tool requests,
summarize logs, and recommend the next experiment. It can also change the
question without noticing, submit an illegal candidate, accept a clean tool
exit that measured nothing, optimize a misleading proxy, or generalize a
result beyond the conditions that produced it. A sequence of prompts and tool
calls does not reveal where any of those failures occurred.

A life cycle makes those failure boundaries explicit. Established systems
engineering processes separate iterative technical work so that teams can
review progress and return to the work that needs revision
[@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook]. This book adapts that principle rather
than its particular process model. The six responsibilities that follow are
this book's synthesis for moving AI-assisted architecture work from design intent
to a reviewed decision:
Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and
Decide. They can repeat, overlap, and return to earlier work. They are not six
agents, six software components, or a waterfall schedule. Each asks a
different question and leaves a different result for the next architect to
inspect.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Explain why ad hoc prompts and tool calls do not constitute an architecture
  design method.
- Distinguish the six life-cycle responsibilities by the question each asks,
  the result it leaves, and the repair it owns.
- Organize work that repeats, branches, or stops without treating the life
  cycle as a waterfall or prescribed team structure.
- Distinguish the complete life cycle, a scoped study, an iterative design
  loop, and the record that preserves the work.
- Preserve enough context for another architect to inspect what ran, what
  failed, what the evidence supports, and what remains unresolved.
:::

## Why AI-Assisted Design Needs a Life Cycle {#sec-arch2-ontology}

Ordinary architecture work is already difficult to reconstruct after the fact.
A simulator configuration may live in one repository, the workload selection
in another, the power assumptions in a spreadsheet, and the reason for a
constraint in a reviewer's notes. Human teams bridge these gaps through shared
history and repeated discussion. An AI system has no reliable access to that
context unless the work makes it explicit.

The need becomes more acute as assistance scales. More candidates do not
automatically produce more knowledge. If ten thousand runs use the wrong
baseline, they repeat one mistake ten thousand times. If a generated RTL block
passes a narrow test but violates an unstated interface requirement, the test
has certified the wrong thing. If an optimizer finds a simulator loophole, its
best score may be the least credible candidate. Expensive simulation and EDA
runs make these errors especially costly because a bad question can consume
hours of compute before anyone discovers that the result cannot support a
decision.

Software engineering offers a useful comparison. SWE-bench defines a bounded
software task by pairing a repository issue with a known repository state and
executable tests [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. Architecture needs comparable
discipline, but no single test settles performance, power, area, timing,
physical feasibility, software behavior, and the system-level decision
together. The relevant feedback also arrives from tools with different costs
and different limits.

Consider two teams studying the same cache with established tools. One might
use gem5, a modular computer-system architecture simulator built on a
discrete-event platform, while another uses FireSim, a field-programmable gate
array (FPGA)-accelerated full-system RTL platform
[@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Either can compare cache
sizes, misses, and execution time. Energy estimates require an attached model
or implementation flow whose assumptions must be stated separately. The tool
choice alone does not say which workload phases count, whether the same
baseline was rerun, which other settings stayed fixed, or whether the result is
meant to select a design for RTL evaluation. Those declarations determine
whether the teams performed the same study.

## Six Responsibilities From Intent to Decision

The six responsibilities are a useful default rather than a taxonomy that
every project must adopt. They remain distinct because different failures need
different repairs. A bad question, an illegal candidate, a tool failure,
an invalid comparison, an unsupported explanation, and an incomplete decision
cannot all be sent back to the same step.

1. **Formulate** translates design intent into a question, requirements,
   objectives, legal changes, planned checks, and an intended decision.
2. **Explore** identifies alternatives worth testing and preserves enough of
   the search to show what was and was not considered.
3. **Implement** makes a candidate executable by the relevant tools and
   establishes that the requested work actually ran. It does not necessarily
   mean producing RTL.
4. **Evaluate** compares valid measurements with the declared requirements and
   objectives.
5. **Interpret and Explain** determines what the result means and whether the
   proposed mechanism accounts for it.
6. **Review and Decide** determines what the accumulated work supports, then
   advances, rejects, revises, or stops.

One prospective, unexecuted cache-capacity decision from the mobile XR
Lighthouse grounds the six responsibilities. The narrow example asks which
cache capacity, if any, should advance to later RTL evaluation. It does not
supply an executed result or stand for the full cross-layer moonshot. The case
is small enough to expose each responsibility, but the same distinctions apply
whether the assistance comes from one model, several agents, conventional
optimization, or a combination of AI and established engineering tools.

Across the full XR moonshot, Formulate preserves workload behavior, software
semantics, interfaces, and physical limits. Explore compares CPU, vector, and
accelerator organizations together with cache, memory, interconnect, and
mapping choices. Implement turns the selected software, simulator, RTL, and
electronic design automation (EDA) work into executable requests. Evaluate
joins functional checks with performance, power, timing, and physical results.
Interpret connects any gain or failure to an architecture mechanism, and Review
selects the authorized next action. The cache study below instantiates these
responsibilities only for a deliberately narrow L2-capacity decision. Its
workload, software, interfaces, organization, and other cross-layer choices
remain fixed context rather than alternatives under exploration.

@fig-ontology-loop is the authoritative process view for this chapter. It
places all six responsibilities in one figure so the reader can keep the whole
life cycle in mind while examining any one part.

![**A six-stage life cycle carries design intent to a reviewed decision.** Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide describe the complete responsibilities. Work can return to the responsibility that owns an inadequate result.](images/ch3-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered responsibilities arranged in two rows. Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide carry one scoped study forward. A return path shows that review can revise the question, while other repairs return to the responsibility that owns the inadequate output."}

One complete pass converts design intent into a scoped plan, legal candidates,
executed tool work, checked results, a supported account, and a reviewed next
action. The return path represents revision rather than a universal loop back
to the beginning. A malformed tool request returns to Implement, while missing
observations may require another evaluation run. Review returns to Formulate
only when it exposes a problem in the question, scope, or requirements.

The boxes divide responsibilities, not time. Exploration and implementation
may alternate thousands of times. Evaluation may reject a candidate and send
the work back to Explore. Interpretation may expose a confounding variable
that requires a new measurement. Review may narrow the question rather than
close the study. A small team can carry all six responsibilities, and a large
team can divide one responsibility among many specialists. A foundation model
or a system composed of agents may help across several boxes, but the boxes do
not prescribe its internal organization.

Four related ideas are easy to confuse.

- **Life cycle:** Names the complete responsibilities needed to move from
  intent to a defensible decision.
- **Scoped study:** Applies those responsibilities to one architecture
  question and one intended decision.
- **Design loop:** Describes an iterative path through the relevant
  responsibilities as the design changes and feedback returns.
- **Study record:** Preserves the question, attempts, observations,
  conclusions, and unresolved issues so another architect can inspect the
  work.

The life cycle is the complete map. A scoped study applies it to one question.
A design loop is a recurrent path through the responsibilities as a design
changes and feedback returns. The study record preserves the work across
those iterations. None is a competing process model.

What architects need is a common unit of work between a broad product goal and
the implementation tools discussed above. @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl
places a scoped architecture study in that position. The figure shows the
container for one application of the life cycle, not another process model.
The study preserves the question, comparison, linked work, and review scope that
let architects interpret otherwise disconnected artifacts and tool results.

![**A scoped architecture study connects intent to implementation evidence.** The study container binds its question and decision to the scope, claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported finding, limits, and named owner.](images/F4d-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing architecture intent and judgment above a scoped architecture study container. The container connects a question and decision, scope and claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported finding, limits, and named owner. Measurements return from implementation tools, and later results may revise the claim or study."}

Architecture intent, models, requirements, and rationale establish the goals,
constraints, and stakes, but they do not yet define a specific comparison. A
scoped study supplies that missing connection. Its question and intended
decision define why the work is being done, while its scope and architectural
claim state what is being investigated.

The study then binds methods and tool returns to that claim. Simulators and
models evaluate architectural behavior, compilers and runtimes expose software
interactions, RTL generators produce implementations, and electronic design
automation (EDA) and signoff tools assess physical properties. Their
measurements become useful only after they return to the original question,
constraints, and known tool limits.

The architectural inference is that a tool output is not yet a decision. A
supported finding also needs explicit limits and an owner for the next action.
If the results expose a faulty assumption or an underspecified comparison, the
study revises the question or claim instead of allowing disconnected tool
outputs to stand in for judgment.

Much of the boundary of an ordinary study can remain tacit. One architect may
know that the baseline cache must be rerun because its old result used an
obsolete memory model. Another may know that initialization frames do not
represent steady operation. A simulator owner may remember which prefetcher
setting was qualified, while a project lead remembers that a larger alternative
was already rejected for area. A useful life cycle makes the assumptions that
can change the comparison, its cost, or its interpretation visible before AI
scales the work around them.

A stage boundary is useful when the work on either side can fail independently
and requires a different repair. @tbl-stage-seams applies that test to the five
adjacent boundaries.

| **Boundary** | **Different questions and outputs** | **Different inadequacy and repair** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate → Explore | Formulate asks what decision the study may support and produces a scoped plan. Explore asks which alternatives exist inside that plan and produces candidates plus a search history. | An inadequate plan returns to the question, scope, or requirements. An inadequate exploration returns to the represented design space or the method used to search it. |
| Explore → Implement | Explore asks which candidate should be tried. Implement asks whether that candidate can be expressed as a valid tool request and whether the requested work ran. | A missing or illegal candidate returns to the design space. A stale workspace, malformed request, license failure, or empty output returns to the tool setup or request. |
| Implement → Evaluate | Implement produces a valid execution record or an infrastructure failure. Evaluate produces a checked comparison. | A run that never executed cannot count against the candidate. A completed run whose result fails a declared check can. |
| Evaluate → Interpret and Explain | Evaluate asks whether the measured result meets the declared requirements and objectives. Interpretation asks what the result means and whether the proposed mechanism produced it. | A measurement problem returns to the measurement plan or candidate. A mechanism problem returns to the hypothesis, retained observations, or contrast used to test it. |
| Interpret and Explain → Review and Decide | Interpretation produces a supported, revised, or contradicted account. Review asks what that account and the checked result permit the study to conclude. | An incomplete explanation returns to the hypothesis or study. An insufficient study record narrows the conclusion, reopens a named responsibility, or stops honestly. |

: **Stage boundaries separate different questions and repairs.** Each row
shows why the work on either side of a boundary can fail independently. When
neither the question nor the repair differs, adjacent responsibilities can be
combined for that project. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[20,41,39]"}

The two middle boundaries show why the distinction matters. Implement must
first establish that the intended work ran; only then can Evaluate judge what
the return says about the candidate. Evaluate can establish a measured result
without establishing the mechanism that produced it, which is why
Interpret and Explain remains separate. In both cases, independently failing
outputs and different repair paths justify the boundary. A project may combine
the work operationally, but it should not erase the distinction when
diagnosing a failure.

Each responsibility must receive enough information to make its own judgment,
leave an inspectable result, and identify the repair when that result is
inadequate. Formulate comes first because legal alternatives and the intended
decision must exist before Explore can propose candidates that anyone can
judge as relevant or admissible.

## Formulating the Architecture Question and Intended Decision

Formulation begins with intent, but intent is not yet a testable architecture
problem. The Lighthouse goal asks for a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V mobile XR
subsystem. It leaves open whether the relevant intervention belongs in the
instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, accelerator, memory
system, compiler, runtime, or their interfaces. It also leaves open what
evidence would justify acting on a proposal.

Refinement preserves that intent while making it progressively testable. A
system-level goal becomes workload and user-facing requirements. Those
requirements become architecture choices and interface obligations. An ISA or
hardware-software interface then constrains what software may assume and what
hardware must provide. An implementation finally exposes measurable timing,
power, area, and correctness properties. Each refinement can add detail, but
it should not silently change the original goal.

<!-- Preserved outside the main flow: images/F4-ontology-chain -->

The prospective XR cache study narrows the broad moonshot to one pre-RTL cache
decision. The question is which, if either, of two larger L2 capacities should
advance to RTL evaluation. @tbl-bounded-study-contract records the plan before
any search method is chosen. The values are illustrative. Their purpose is to
show which declarations make the comparison and its limits inspectable.

| **Declaration** | **Prospective mobile XR cache study** |
| --- | --- |
| Question | Which, if either, of the 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation for the declared XR workload? |
| Comparator | The current 2\ MiB L2 baseline. Both larger candidates are compared against the same rerun baseline. |
| Scope | One cache-capacity decision inside the compute subsystem. Cache policy, network-on-chip topology, compiler, runtime, and the rest of the memory system remain fixed. |
| Permitted changes | L2 capacity may take the values 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, or 4\ MiB. No other architecture parameter may change in this study. |
| Hard constraints | Modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power must not exceed 3\ W. The cache macro must not exceed 1.5\ mm^2^, and its modeled access time must not exceed the 2.5\ ns, or five-cycle, allocation used by the 2\ GHz microarchitecture. Required thermal and resistive voltage-drop (IR-drop) review remains independent. |
| Objectives and tradeoffs | Reduce 99th-percentile frame time while limiting added power and area. A candidate that improves tail latency at higher cost remains a tradeoff alternative rather than an automatic winner. |
| Conditions | A versioned workload snapshot, including stable frame identifiers and boundaries; a versioned RISC-V software image; and recorded versions of the cycle-level simulator, cache model, power model, static random-access memory (SRAM) model, and process, voltage, and temperature assumptions. |
| Planned measurements and checks | Run the same functional regression suite for every capacity, require identical ISA-visible outputs for the declared test inputs, and require no failure from the simulator's coherence-invariant checks. Measure 99th-percentile frame time, cache misses by classification including capacity misses, dynamic and leakage power, macro area, and access time while retaining stable frame identifiers. Estimate the frame-time reduction and quantify its uncertainty over matched baseline and candidate frame observations. A capacity advances only if its functional and physical checks pass and the comparison relative to 2\ MiB remains above zero under the declared uncertainty check. |
| Budget | Four cycle-level executions in total, including reruns after infrastructure failures, plus one SRAM timing, area, and power evaluation per declared capacity. No RTL synthesis or physical signoff is included. |
| Stopping conditions | Stop when the intended decision is resolved, all permitted capacities are exhausted, the run budget is spent, or a required input or measurement remains unavailable. |
| Intended decision | Recommend at most one cache capacity for a later RTL study. This plan does not authorize implementation, signoff, tapeout, or a product commitment. |
| Exclusions | Cache policy, prefetching, coherence, network-on-chip changes, compiler changes, software scheduling, full floorplanning, thermal signoff, IR-drop signoff, security, reliability, and product-level cost. |

: **A scoped plan declares the comparison before a method is chosen.** The
question and legal design space determine the requirements and planned
observations, while the remaining rows bound the cost and decision the study
may support. {#tbl-bounded-study-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Hard constraints and tradeoff objectives play different roles. A hard
constraint rules out a candidate. A design that misses timing is not rescued
by excellent energy efficiency. An objective ranks or compares candidates that
remain feasible. Power, area, latency, and implementation effort may pull in
different directions. Those declarations allow Explore to return the Pareto
set introduced in @tbl-moonshot-decomposition, preserving feasible tradeoffs
rather than declaring one universal winner [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

The table's tail-latency objective is intentional. The XRBench workload anchor
includes real-time deadlines and quality-of-experience constraints
[@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. A cache that improves mean instructions per cycle while
lengthening the slowest frames can be a system-level regression. The plan
therefore retains stable frame identifiers and requires an
uncertainty-qualified comparison against the rerun 2\ MiB baseline. The
statistical mechanics of that comparison belong to the feedback and evaluation
treatment in @sec-feedback-verification-trust. Here Formulate must declare the
observations and advancement rule before any candidate is explored.

An architectural claim makes the expected result falsifiable.

> **Architectural claim.** An architectural claim states the proposed
> mechanism, expected outcome, scenario, comparator, alternatives,
> requirements, and evidence that would count against it.

For this study, the claim is that at least one larger L2 reduces
99th-percentile frame time relative to the 2\ MiB baseline because it removes
capacity misses while remaining inside the declared power, area, and timing
constraints. The claim does not assume that fewer misses necessarily reduce
frame time. It makes that connection something the measurements must test.

Requirements must remain traceable as the study proceeds. The 3\ W requirement,
for example, becomes a subsystem power allocation under recorded activity and
model assumptions, then an acceptance check on dynamic plus leakage power. A
change to the software image, activity, power model, or voltage assumptions
invalidates that result and reopens the check. Functional obligations follow a
separate trace. Varying cache capacity does not permit a candidate to change
the declared coherence behavior, memory semantics, or ISA-visible software
result, so the plan must name the functional check that preserves them.

Formulate should also declare cheap bounds that Explore can apply before any
simulator is invoked. If the frames that set the tail spend 18 percent of their
latency stalled on L2 capacity misses, eliminating every one of those stalls
can recover at most that fraction for those observations. This Amdahl-style
upper bound [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor] cannot select a cache size, but
it can reject a claim that asks the named mechanism for more improvement than
the workload contains.

Requirements also need units and conditions. A 3\ W limit and a 2\ GHz target
do not identify the power components, workload state, process corner, voltage,
temperature, or guardband under which they must hold. Coupled effects such as
cache banking, interconnect distance, floorplan blockage, power delivery, and
temperature remain visible whenever they could reverse the comparison.

NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter mishap shows why the interface is part of the
requirement. Its navigation interface required newton-seconds, but ground
software supplied pound-force seconds [@MCOMishapBoard1999]. Each component
ran, yet no check caught the mismatch where the value was consumed. The 4.45
conversion error accumulated until the reconstructed closest approach was 57
km, below the planned 226 km and the estimated survivable minimum of 80 km. A
written requirement becomes operational only when the work names its units and
conditions and assigns the check at the consuming interface. A clean run cannot
repair a missing interface check.

Formulate ends by handing Explore the declared legal space, checks, and decision
bounds. Explore can propose alternatives within that space, but it cannot
silently change the question, requirements, or interfaces that make the
comparison meaningful.

## Exploring Alternatives Within the Declared Space

Exploration asks which alternatives are worth testing inside the legal design
space that Formulate declared. Its adequacy depends on the intended decision,
the represented space, and the available budget. A sweep that is sufficient to
nominate an early candidate may be insufficient to support a claim that the
important alternatives were examined.

The output is therefore more than a candidate list. The exploration record
should expose which consequential regions or boundary cases were examined,
which regions were pruned by an already established valid check, and what
remains unexplored. It should also state whether the work supports the intended
decision or merely nominates candidates for later testing. An illegal candidate
or an inadequate search returns to the represented design space or search
method rather than passing to implementation.

The simplest method is often the right one. The prospective XR cache study has
only three legal cache capacities, so direct enumeration completely covers the
declared 2, 3, and 4\ MiB choices. It is clearer than a learned method and is a
credible no-AI choice. That coverage says nothing about capacities or cache
policies excluded during Formulate. Larger spaces may justify prediction,
generation, optimization, or a combination, but method choice does not change
the responsibility. A large candidate count is not evidence that consequential
regions were covered.

Legal does not mean independent. Increasing cache capacity can change access
time, banking, interconnect distance, leakage, floorplan pressure, and the
software-visible benefit of another optimization. Exploration therefore works
with coupled alternatives rather than a bag of unrelated parameters. It must
also preserve interface and software assumptions so that a candidate does not
win by changing something the study declared fixed.

These couplings extend beyond cache capacity. A change in the instruction set
architecture (ISA) or vector width can change compiler lowering and runtime
mapping. Moving work into an accelerator can change memory traffic,
interconnect load, floorplan, and timing. Exploration should preserve why it
sampled or pruned each region and which dependency drove that choice. If a
coupling changes a declared workload, interface, constraint, or legal action,
Explore cannot absorb it silently. The study returns to Formulate so the design
space and checks can be revised.

Explore can use cheap checks already established for the represented state. If
measured XR observations support the illustrative 18 percent stall fraction,
the Amdahl-style bound from Formulate can show that a claim asks the named
mechanism for more improvement than the workload contains. A new SRAM-model
execution is different. Explore nominates the capacity, Implement runs the
requested model, and Evaluate checks the timing result. A failed checked result
can then return to Explore to update the candidate set. Explore may prioritize
or prune only on checks whose validity has already been established for the
current study conditions.

For the cache study, Explore produces two new candidates, 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB, plus
the rerun 2\ MiB baseline. Exploration can stop when every declared capacity has
been enumerated and each legal candidate has either advanced, been excluded by
an already established check, or returned from Evaluate with a checked failure.
A larger space would need a coverage or budget-based stop that fits its intended
decision. The result is a defensible candidate set and a record of its limits.
Explore constructs and narrows that set. It does not find or certify the answer.

## Implementing a Testable Candidate

Implementation makes a selected candidate executable by the intended tools. In an
AI-assisted setting, this may mean generating RTL, modifying simulator
parameters, constructing a workload, writing a compiler transformation, or
preparing a sequence of EDA tool commands. The essential result is not code or
a command file by itself. It is a candidate that the intended tools can
actually test under the declared conditions.

Each tool request must preserve the candidate's identity and the study state.
For the prospective XR cache study, the request must name the cache parameters,
baseline software image, workload trace, clocks, process assumptions, and
expected outputs. It must also confirm that the tool used them. A syntactically
valid configuration can still select the wrong top level, reuse stale constraints,
or skip the workload region that defines the comparison.

This creates a crucial distinction between an infrastructure failure and a
candidate failure. A crash, license timeout, stale workspace, malformed timing
constraint, empty netlist, or clean exit that analyzed no paths says that the
requested test did not run correctly. It says nothing about the quality of the
candidate. Only a valid execution can produce a result that later rejects a
design.

For the cache study, the 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB capacities must become valid
SRAM model and cycle-level simulator requests. If an inexpensive SRAM check
runs first, Implement must confirm that its area and access-time outputs
describe the intended capacity and conditions before passing them to Evaluate.
The detailed mechanics of tool isolation, retry, recovery, and interface design
belong to environment engineering. At the life-cycle level, the handoff is
simple. Either the intended work ran and produced qualified outputs, or the
attempt remains an infrastructure failure. That failure returns to Implement
for a repaired request or tool setup and does not reject the candidate.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The tool reported a chip that did not exist"}
**The trap.** An automated search reports 0.0\ W and 0.0\ mm^2^ with a
successful tool exit.

**The mechanism.** The request selected no valid top-level design and omitted
the primary clock. Elaboration contained none of the expected instances,
timing analysis had no constrained paths, and a downstream parser substituted
zeros for absent power and area fields.

**The lesson.** This is an infrastructure failure, not a breakthrough and not
a rejected candidate. A useful implementation check confirms that the expected
clocks, instances, paths, and outputs exist before evaluation interprets their
numbers.

This is a composite of a recurring tool-flow failure pattern rather than one
published incident.
:::

## Evaluating the Candidate Against Declared Checks

Evaluation begins only after implementation establishes that the intended work
ran. It compares the returned measurements with the requirements, objectives,
and validity conditions declared during formulation. The result is not merely
a score. It states which checks passed, which failed, which remain unresolved,
and how much confidence the available measurements justify.

The prospective XR cache study first requires the declared functional
regression and coherence checks to pass, then applies the hard physical checks.
A cache macro outside the 1.5\ mm^2^ area limit, beyond the 2.5\ ns access-time
allocation, or above the 3\ W subsystem envelope is rejected even if it improves
frame time. A feasible candidate then faces the tail-latency comparison with
the rerun 2\ MiB baseline. A reduction in capacity misses does not substitute
for a resolved frame-time result because the claim names both the mechanism and
the system-level outcome.

Cost and fidelity shape the order of evaluation. An analytic estimate or SRAM
model may reject a candidate before a cycle-level run, and simulation may
precede RTL or physical analysis. A model can be inaccurate in absolute values
yet still preserve the difference between a baseline and candidate or their
ranking. The study must validate the property its decision uses over the
relevant candidate region. One accuracy number cannot establish every kind of
comparison.

Higher fidelity can strengthen an answer to the declared question when its
assumptions and validation support the comparison. It does not widen the
decision scope. A cycle-level result does not authorize RTL implementation if
the study promised only a recommendation for further evaluation, and an RTL
result does not waive thermal, IR-drop, reliability, or product review that the
study excluded.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Passing the power check would not decide the study"}
**Context.** A power result becomes useful only when a reviewer can see which
workload, candidate, tool state, software assumptions, and power components it
describes.

**In this prospective study.** A valid future run that passed the declared
power check would satisfy only that check. The intended decision would still
depend on a resolved tail-latency comparison and later independent physical
review. Passing one check cannot resolve another.
:::

An evaluation can therefore end in several legitimate states. An invalid
execution returns to Implement, while a comparison that lacks required
observations returns to Evaluate. A valid result may reject a candidate. The
measurement may be too uncertain to distinguish two candidates, the run budget
may expire, or required data may be unavailable. These states determine
different next actions and must remain visible to review.

## Interpreting and Explaining the Result

Evaluation asks whether a result clears the declared checks. Interpretation
asks what the result means, while explanation asks whether the proposed
mechanism accounts for it. A favorable number can pass evaluation and still
fail this responsibility.

Suppose the 3\ MiB cache reduces capacity misses and improves
99th-percentile frame time. The result is consistent with the claim, but it
does not yet establish the mechanism. The larger cache may also change hit
latency, memory-level parallelism, prefetch behavior, or contention. Stable
frame identifiers, miss classifications, and relevant pipeline or memory
telemetry let the architect connect the measured outcome to a physical account
instead of relying on a plausible narrative.

Gupta and colleagues provide a useful warning. They used an evolutionary
coding agent to write last-level cache replacement policies for ChampSim
[@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim; @GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. One generated policy appeared
to improve instructions per cycle by bypassing writes that then disappeared
from the modeled memory system. The simulator score improved, but the gain did
not come from a valid cache mechanism. Inspection of the generated policy and
simulator behavior exposed the loophole.

That case does not mean every result needs an elaborate causal proof. It means
that a metric and its mechanism are different claims. A direct physical check
may explain a simple violation. More coupled behavior may require a contrast,
counterfactual, or ablation. The planned level of explanation should match the
consequence of the decision and the ways the evaluation setup can be exploited.

The needed observations should be chosen before the expensive run whenever
possible. A top-line score cannot recover miss classifications or per-frame
histories that the run discarded. For the prospective XR cache study, the
expected output is an account of whether reduced capacity misses occur in the
frames that shape the tail and whether they explain the frame-time change. The
account may support both the mechanism and the outcome, support only one, or
leave both unresolved. Missing observations return to Evaluate, while a
contradicted mechanism returns to the claim. Fluent prose can organize the
account, but it cannot replace the measurements that support it or extend the
result beyond the recorded workload and tool conditions.

## Reviewing the Result and Choosing the Next Action

Review brings the scoped plan and all subsequent work back together. The
architect asks whether the legal alternatives were explored adequately,
whether the intended tools ran, whether the measurements satisfy the declared
checks, whether the explanation is credible, and whether the accumulated work
supports the intended decision.

The result is not always approval. Review may advance one candidate, reject a
candidate, request another comparison, revise the question, narrow the
conclusion, or stop because the budget or available information is exhausted.
An honest unresolved result is a useful outcome when the study record makes
clear why the question remains open.

In the prospective XR cache study, review may advance the 3\ MiB or 4\ MiB
capacity to RTL evaluation, reject both when a declared check fails, or request
another comparison when the tail-latency result or proposed mechanism remains
unresolved. If the budget is exhausted before any option is supported, the
study stops without a recommendation.

The study's scoped review and next action are complete only when every required
result has a disposition, the supported action remains inside the declared
scope, and the study record names what would reopen the work. This completion
does not authorize an architecture or product commitment. A study stops
honestly when the budget, available evidence, or remaining legal alternatives
cannot justify another useful action. It does not quietly convert an exhausted
search into acceptance.

Putting the stage results beside their repair paths reveals whether missing
evidence calls for a new candidate, a repaired execution, another measurement,
or a narrower decision (@tbl-stage-contracts).

| **Stage** | **Receives** | **Produces and checks** | **Repair and handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate | Product intent, a design question, known requirements, and applicable downstream checks. | A scoped plan whose question, comparator, objectives, constraints, conditions, measurements, budget, stop, decision, and exclusions agree. | Repair the question or scope. Hand the plan to Explore without choosing a method prematurely. |
| Explore | The scoped plan, represented legal changes, and any previously established checks. | One or more legal candidates, their selection history, and the limits of the explored region. | Repair the design space or search approach. Hand a named candidate to Implement; use checked failures returned by Evaluate to update the candidate set. |
| Implement | A candidate, requested tool work, budget, and required inputs. | An execution record showing the requested work ran on the intended state, or a recorded infrastructure failure showing that it did not. | Repair the request or tool setup. Hand completed tool returns to Evaluate. Never treat an unevaluated candidate as rejected. |
| Evaluate | Completed tool returns, comparator, planned metrics, thresholds, and validity conditions. | A comparison stating which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved, together with the observations needed for interpretation. | Repair the measurement plan, rerun within budget, or reject the candidate on a declared check. |
| Interpret and Explain | The checked result, proposed mechanism, and retained observations. | An account supported, revised, or contradicted by a declared contrast, ablation, or direct physical reason. | Repair the hypothesis or request missing observations. Hand the result and mechanism status to review. |
| Review and Decide | The scoped plan and study record from all prior work. | A decision within the declared scope, a narrower conclusion, a named revision, or an honest stop with unresolved questions. | Reopen the work that owns the missing result or close the study. Preserve the reason for the action. |

: **Each responsibility produces something another architect can inspect.** The
table summarizes inputs, outputs, and repair paths without prescribing a
specific model, method, tool interface, or team organization.
{#tbl-stage-contracts tbl-colwidths="[15,25,34,26]"}

The rows connect what each responsibility receives to the result another
architect can inspect and the repair needed when that result is inadequate.
The Implement and Evaluate rows give the decisive contrast. A tool
request must first establish that the intended work ran before its numbers can
pass or fail an architecture check. Review uses these handoffs to decide where
any missing result must return.

Review and Decide may choose only actions the project has authorized. The
accountable organization is the project organization that assigns those
decision rights. Review verifies that the actor taking the next action is
authorized and that the action remains inside the delegated scope. A system may
be allowed to propose a candidate, execute a declared test, reject a candidate
when a mechanical check fails, or recommend a next step. Waiving a requirement
and committing the project to a costly or irreversible action are different
rights. They remain with named people who accept the residual risk. Neither the
system nor the review activity can assign or enlarge its own authority.

When review calls for revision, it must name the responsibility that reopens
and preserve the requirements, candidate, tool conditions, and prior results
from which the repaired work proceeds.

## Iteration, Revision, and State

Revision is not a seventh stage. When an output is inadequate, the work returns
to the responsibility that owns the repair. A malformed tool request returns to
Implement without changing the candidate. An unexplained frame-time gain may
return to Evaluate for more observations or to Interpret and Explain for a
better mechanism test. A changed product requirement reopens Formulate.

When those returns recur, a design loop keeps each change connected to the
original question and next decision. Agile RISC-V development and reusable
generator-based hardware construction provide one lineage for this kind of
iteration [@LeeEtAl2016AgileRISCV; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. The loop in
@fig-design-loop is one recurrent path through the six life-cycle
responsibilities, not a peer process taxonomy.

![**A design loop revisits the life-cycle responsibility that owns each repair.** One pass carries the outputs of Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide. A named repair returns to the responsible stage, while a supported result reaches a scoped outcome.](images/F3-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="82%" fig-alt="Six life-cycle responsibilities shown as one recurrent path through a scoped plan, legal candidate, execution record, checked result, supported account, and next action. Review either produces a scoped outcome or a named repair that returns to the responsible stage."}

The loop starts with the scoped plan that Formulate leaves. Explore adds a
legal candidate and its selection history. Implement adds an execution record
or records a tool failure. Evaluate produces a checked result, and Interpret
and Explain produces an account of its support and mechanism. Review and Decide
then names the next action. If the result is inadequate, the return path records
which responsibility must act next and why. A rejected 4\ MiB cache may return
to Explore, while an infrastructure failure returns to Implement without
counting against that candidate.

Parallel branches use the same state discipline. Each branch names the study
revision it used and binds its actions and results to that revision. Results
can be merged only after their assumptions, interfaces, and permitted changes
are checked for compatibility. If one branch changes a shared requirement,
model, or interface, affected results in other branches require revalidation.
This is the same change-control obligation that systems engineering places on
versioned technical work. A revision must identify what changed and trigger
revalidation of affected requirements, interfaces, and verification results
[@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook].

Machine-learning systems provide a useful precedent for this problem. A local
component change can create hidden dependencies and feedback loops across data,
models, and surrounding software [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. In an architecture
study, a new cache surrogate can change which candidates are simulated, and
those simulator results may then become the surrogate's next training data.
Architecture extends the problem across costly tool fidelities and into
physical consequences. The software lesson exposes the dependency, but it does
not establish that a cache conclusion survives a new tool fidelity or physical
implementation.

This binding also preserves useful learning. A rejected cache capacity can
inform later work only when its workload, tool versions, process assumptions,
and failed check remain attached. A change that invalidates the result does not
erase it, but it prevents the result from silently carrying forward as current
evidence.

A proxy, simulation, or higher-fidelity check may strengthen the answer to the
declared question. Raising measurement fidelity may strengthen the answer, but
it cannot enlarge decision authority. A stronger measurement cannot change who
may commit the design or waive an independent requirement.

## A Design-Loop Card for Review

Architecture teams already retain requirements, experiment results, regression
and coverage data, signoff reports, issues, and change records in project
systems. A design-loop card does not replace those systems or prescribe a
universal form. It provides a compact index into the artifacts that bear on one
scoped architecture question and the decision the work is meant to support.

The card borrows the reporting instinct behind model cards and datasheets for
datasets, which make intended use, evaluation conditions, and known limits
reviewable [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. The analogy
has a limit. An architecture study must also preserve the changing design state,
tool conditions, physical assumptions, failed checks, and the authority for the
next action. A static description of a model or dataset cannot carry those
responsibilities by itself.

A study record makes the state and its revisions inspectable.

> **Study record.** The cumulative account of one scoped architecture study.
> It retains the plan, stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved
> questions, stopping reason, and supported decision, with links to the
> detailed artifacts needed for review or replay.

For each consequential transition, the study record names the study revision,
who or what proposed and approved the action, what executed it, what checked the
result, and what later change would invalidate it. The record keeps the links
to existing engineering artifacts current rather than copying their contents.
Scientific workflow preservation offers a precedent for binding an analysis to
versioned inputs, software, parameters, and provenance so another researcher can
inspect or replay it [@ChenEtAl2016CERNAnalysisPreservation]. Architecture needs
that replay information, but it also needs the decision being supported, the
physical assumptions and failed checks that bound the result, and the named
authority that may act on it.

The design-loop card in @fig-filled-design-loop-card is an optional compact
index into that record. The filled example stays with the XR cache-capacity
study rather than introducing a second design problem.

![**An optional study card separates support from decision.** The cache example connects intent and scope to methods, checks, results, and rejected alternatives. Its final row keeps what the evidence supports separate from the accountable decision.](images/F4b-design-loop-card-example){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="84%" fig-alt="An optional filled study card for the XR cache-capacity comparison. A claim under review appears above fields for the 2 MiB baseline, 3 MiB and 4 MiB candidates, direct enumeration, tool and feedback conditions, failed runs, rejection checks, evidence support, and the accountable decision."}

The claim at the top anchors the fields below. The middle rows point to work
planned or performed and distinguish infrastructure failures from candidates
rejected by declared checks. The final row keeps evidence support separate from the
accountable decision. An unresolved comparison or budget stop remains visible
rather than being recast as a completed decision. The card is one compact view
of the study record, not a required artifact and not a substitute for the linked
engineering records.

## Open Questions

The life cycle proposed in this chapter must remain useful under different
design stakes, failure combinations, and volumes of machine-generated work.

**Repair and reviewable state.** When several responsibilities fail together,
the study must decide where repair begins and which failed work remains useful
to later review.

- **How should an AI-assisted study route repair when several life-cycle
  responsibilities are inadequate at once?** Repairing the most visible symptom
  can repeat expensive invalid work while other failures remain. A useful result
  would reduce invalid reruns, time to a valid result, or expensive tool use
  without hiding unresolved failures.

- **Which failed attempts should remain part of the reviewable state of an
  AI-assisted architecture study?** Keeping too little hides causes and invites
  repeated failure, while keeping everything makes review and maintenance
  impractical. Retention choices can be judged by repeated failures prevented,
  missed causes, review time, and cost while preserving the conditions that
  bound each failure.

**Proportionate structure and independent review.** A life cycle should prevent
silent changes to the design question and preserve credible review without
imposing tapeout-level work on every early exploration.

- **What evidence can reveal that an architecture question has changed silently
  as a study moves across life-cycle responsibilities?** The comparator,
  workload, constraint, or acceptance condition may shift while the resulting
  artifacts still appear compatible. The open problem is catching material
  changes before they cause invalid downstream work without treating every
  revision as a new study.

- **How should life-cycle structure change as an architecture decision becomes
  more costly or harder to reverse?** Early exploration and architecture
  commitment should not require identical records or reviews. The unresolved
  problem is how to strengthen evidence and review as consequences increase
  without losing traceability or imposing unnecessary work.

- **How can architects review studies in which the same AI system proposed
  candidates, selected measurements, and generated explanations?** Separate
  prompts or named roles may still share the same model, context, and failure
  modes. The research problem is to determine which responsibility boundaries
  require independent evidence or decision rights and how that separation
  changes missed errors and review cost.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Separate responsibilities when failures need different repairs"}
Organize AI-assisted architecture work around the question each responsibility
answers, the result it leaves, and the repair it owns. Keep responsibilities
distinct when their outputs can fail independently. When a result is
inadequate, return the work to the responsibility that can repair it without
losing the question, candidate, tool conditions, or prior results.
:::

The AI-assisted design life cycle organizes the complete path from intent to a
reviewed architecture decision. Formulate turns a broad goal into testable
requirements, objectives, legal alternatives, and an intended decision.
Explore finds candidates inside that space. Implement makes a candidate
testable and distinguishes valid work from infrastructure failure. Evaluate
applies the declared checks. Interpret and Explain connect the measured result
to an architecture mechanism and its limits. Review and Decide determine what
the cumulative work supports and whether to advance, reject, revise, or stop.

These responsibilities are neither a waterfall nor an agent architecture.
They can repeat, overlap, and return to the work that needs repair. Their
purpose is to keep different failures from collapsing into one unsuccessful
run. A malformed invocation is not a rejected design. A favorable score is not
an explanation. A higher-fidelity measurement is not broader authority. A
budget stop is not a completed decision.

The prospective XR cache example showed how one scoped study uses the complete
life cycle. Its broad system goal became a narrow decision about which cache
capacity, if any, should advance to RTL evaluation. Hard constraints remained
separate from tradeoff objectives. Tail latency stayed connected to the
real-time workload. Tool requests had to establish that the intended design
ran before any number could reject a candidate. The final study record preserved open questions and
decision limits rather than filling them in after the fact.

The durable lesson is larger than the example. AI-assisted architecture design
needs a way to preserve intent as work crosses models, methods, software,
hardware descriptions, simulators, and physical tools. The life cycle supplies
that common structure. It lets AI do more of the work without allowing the
speed or fluency of the system to become a substitute for engineering
judgment.

That structure can operate only when the study has usable data, current
project knowledge, and representations that preserve the design relationships
the work depends on. @sec-data-representations-world-models develops
those requirements without assuming that one representation can serve every
stage.
